# Research Memorandum: Implementable Cognitive Mechanisms in *Learnability and Cognition*, File Pages 1 through 163

## Scope and Extraction Status

This section is substantive argument, not apparatus. File pages 1 through 11 carry title matter and the table of contents. File pages 12 through 21 contain the series foreword, the preface to the new edition, and acknowledgments. File pages 22 through 73 present chapter 1, the statement of Baker's paradox and the failure of proposed solutions. File pages 74 through 92 present chapter 2, the morphological and semantic criteria that govern lexical rules and the problems those criteria create. File pages 94 through 135 present chapter 3, the theory that lexical rules operate on semantic structures and that argument structures follow from linking rules. File pages 136 through 163 present the opening of chapter 4, on narrow conflation classes and the problem of negative exceptions. The section ends mid-discussion of the morphological constraint on the dative. I have not cited beyond file page 163.

The extraction contains one figure that matters for my job. File page 95 carries a diagram contrasting the old theory of lexical rules, in which a rule changes argument structure and semantic constraints filter its application, with the new theory, in which a rule changes semantic structure and linking rules project argument structure from it. The diagram is rendered as text fragments in the extraction, so I can report its logic from the surrounding prose but cannot verify its exact graphical layout. File page 116 carries a second diagram summarizing the locative alternation, again partially garbled. I flag both as extraction gaps.

## The Central Problem and Why It Constrains Any Machine

Pinker's problem is not how to classify verbs. It is how a learner can generalize productively while the language it is learning contains exceptions to every generalization, and while the learner receives no reliable signal about which forms are ungrammatical. File page 27 states the logical structure of the problem: infinitely many hypotheses fit a finite sample, and a hypothesis that generates a superset of the target language cannot be falsified by positive evidence alone. File page 28 reports that parents do not differentially approve or disapprove of children's grammatical versus ungrammatical utterances, citing Brown and Hanlon. File pages 32 through 37 examine the claim that subtle feedback such as repetitions or recasts supplies negative evidence, and Pinker argues it does not: the feedback is noisy, not uniformly contingent on ungrammaticality, not available to every child, and not demonstrably used by children. File page 35 gives the concrete example of a child who says "Nobody don't like me" and resists eight rounds of overt correction.

This matters for a thinking machine because it rules out a large family of learning designs. A machine that learns by trial and error with external correction is not modeling the problem Pinker describes. A machine that stores every observed form and refuses to generalize is refuted by the productivity data. File pages 42 through 51 document children producing passives, double-object datives, causatives, and locatives with invented verbs they never heard in those forms. File page 54 reports elicitation rates: productive passives at nineteen to eighty-one percent of opportunities, double-object datives at forty to fifty-three percent, lexical causatives at fifty-five to sixty-six percent, and container-object locatives at seventy-eight to one hundred percent. File page 54 also reports a control condition in which children were exposed to a pseudoargument structure and produced it only four percent of the time, against fifty percent for the double-object form. That control is important: it shows children are not simply complying with experimental demand.

## What Must Be Built In and What Can Be Learned

Pinker's answer, developed across file pages 81 through 135, is that the learner is constrained by the format of its representations and by the operations that act on them. The constraints are not arbitrary filters appended to rules. They fall out of what the rules do to semantic structures.

File page 95 states the core proposal: a lexical rule takes a semantic structure as input and produces a new semantic structure as output. Argument structures are then projected from semantic structures by linking rules. The semantic change is what makes the rule selective. Dativization converts "cause X to go to Y" into "cause Y to have X" (file page 96). Causativization converts "Y changes" into "cause Y to change" (file page 96). Locativization converts "cause X to go into or onto Y" into "cause Y to change state by means of putting X into or onto it" (file pages 96 through 97). Passivization converts "X acts on Y" into "Y is in the circumstance of X acting on it" (file page 97).

For an implementable machine, this means the following. The stored data is a semantic structure: a structured record with named participant slots and elementary predicates such as cause, go, be, have, act, and to. File page 107 lists these as the semantic elements for now, and file page 108 explains that thematic roles are not atomic labels but positions in a structured representation. The elementary operation is a transformation on that record: it adds, suppresses, or redescribes arguments. The output is a new semantic record. A second operation, the linking rule, maps open arguments onto grammatical functions. File pages 108 through 109 give the first approximation: the first argument of cause links to subject, the second argument of cause links to object, the first argument of be or go links to subject if unlinked and to object otherwise, the argument of to links to oblique, and the third argument of cause-to-have links to second object. The biuniqueness constraint, that every open argument links to exactly one function and no function receives more than one argument, is stated at file page 108.

These are implementable as data structures and pattern-matching operations. What I supply myself is the engineering decision to represent each semantic structure as a record with typed slots, each linking rule as a function from slot to grammatical role, and each lexical rule as a rewrite on records. Pinker does not specify a programming language or data format. He specifies the logical form of the representations and the direction of the operations.

## Composition, Role Binding, and the Autonomy of Lexical Semantics

File pages 146 through 148 make a claim that is decisive for any machine that tries to learn from perception. Verb meanings are not scripts, frames, stereotypes, or clusters of features computed by general cognitive similarity. They are constraints on which aspects of an event the verb is choosy about. File page 147 gives the example: the semantics of kiss do not require prior motion resulting in contact, even though the typical kissing scenario includes it. The semantics of break do not require that the break be caused by motion followed by contact. What matters is what the semantic representation imposes conditions on, not what typically happens.

This is a material obstacle for a machine grounded in raw sensory data. A machine that clusters events by statistical similarity will group kiss with hug and break with shatter in ways that do not predict syntactic behavior. The machine needs a representation that marks which aspects of an event are constrained and which are left open. File page 146 calls this the autonomy of lexical semantics. My engineering proposal is that each semantic record carry explicit constraint fields alongside open fields, and that the learning operation that assigns a verb to a conflation class inspect only the constraint fields. This is my addition. Pinker describes the distinction but does not give an algorithm for extracting constraint fields from perceptual experience.

## Narrow Conflation Classes and the Limits of Coarse Criteria

File pages 136 through 142 introduce the problem that defeats the simple criteria theory. Coarse semantic criteria are necessary but not sufficient. File page 137 gives the contrasts: throw Mary the ball is grammatical but carry Mary the ball is not; ask Mary a question is grammatical but shout Mary a question is not. File page 138 argues that appealing to subtle meaning differences does not solve the learning problem, because the learner would have to know the relevant meaning component before hearing the verb in the target construction, which is exactly what conservatism would require.

Pinker's solution is narrow conflation classes. File page 142 states that broad conflation classes provide necessary conditions and narrow conflation classes provide sufficient conditions. File pages 143 through 145 demonstrate this with transitive action verbs. The conative alternation applies to verbs of motion followed by contact, such as hit and cut, but not to verbs of touching or breaking. The part-possessor ascension applies to verbs of contact but not breaking. The contact locative applies to verbs of motion followed by contact but not to verbs that specify an effect. The middle applies to verbs specifying an effect. The anticausative applies to verbs specifying an effect but nothing else. File page 145 gives the summary table.

For a machine, this means the lexicon cannot be a flat list of verbs with one argument structure each. It must be a structured inventory of subclasses, where subclass membership is determined by which semantic elements are present in the verb's constraint fields. File page 146 lists motion, contact, and effect as the recurring elements. My proposal is that the machine store for each verb a set of semantic elements drawn from a small vocabulary, and that each lexical rule carry a specification of which element combinations it licenses. The rule fires only when the input verb's element set matches. This is a direct implementation of what Pinker describes, though the exact matching algorithm is mine.

## The Gap Between Computational Possibility and Practical Discovery

File pages 149 through 163 show that even with narrow classes, negative exceptions persist. File page 137 lists verbs that should alternate by coarse criteria but do not. File page 138 concedes that semantic compatibility alone cannot rule them out, and notes dialect differences: Georgia Green finds shout him the answer and carry him the box grammatical in her dialect. This is a real problem for any machine. If the criterion is semantic compatibility, two machines with the same semantic knowledge should make the same judgments. If they do not, the criterion is underspecified.

Pinker's response is that language guards its verbs' grammatically relevant semantic structures vigilantly (file page 140). New meanings can be assigned to old verbs only in precise circumstances, defined by narrow classes. File page 141 gives the example: verbs of instantaneous imparting of force causing ballistic motion can be reconstrued as causing possession, but verbs of continuous exertion of force causing accompanied motion cannot, even though both are cognitively compatible with a change of possession. The distinction is not cognitive but linguistic.

For a machine, this is the hardest part. The machine must learn which narrow classes exist in the language it is acquiring, and the boundaries of those classes are partly arbitrary. File page 148 acknowledges this: the conditions characterizing the set of narrow classes are motivated but not deducible a priori from universal principles. File page 148 suggests that historical processes favor the addition and retention of verbs whose meanings exemplify the semantic structure created by the rule. This is a claim about language change, not about a learning algorithm. It leaves the discovery problem open.

My proposal is that the machine maintain a hypothesis space of candidate narrow classes, defined by combinations of semantic elements, and revise that hypothesis space when it encounters verbs that violate its current class boundaries. File page 82 describes a learning sequence that does something like this: record argument structures, note recurring patterns, create productive rules, note verbs that fail to occur in one form, search for a property that distinguishes the two groups, constrain the rule, and replace the constraint if falsified. This sequence is Pinker's, stated at file page 82. What I supply is the representation of the hypothesis space as a lattice of element combinations and the search procedure over that lattice. Pinker does not specify how the search is conducted or how large the space is. File page 91 notes that the list of possible criteria must be finite and not too large, or the child might never find the relevant one, and concedes that it is difficult to come up with an explicit list.

## Grounding, Temporal Experience, and the Limits of This Section

This section does not address perception directly, except through the claim at file page 140 that perception and cognition are flexible and that most situations can be construed in many ways. File page 140 gives the example of hitting a wall with a stick: is the wall the affected entity and the stick the instrument, or is the stick the affected entity because it moves? The machine must resolve this ambiguity before it can assign a verb to a conflation class. Pinker says language dictates which analysis the speaker is permitted to use, but he does not say how the perceptual system produces the candidate analyses in the first place.

Temporal experience is not discussed in this section. The verbs studied are event verbs, and the semantic structures encode causal and spatial relations, but there is no account of how a machine would store a sequence of observations or use past experience to resolve present ambiguity. This is a gap I must flag rather than fill.

## Unresolved Questions

The next reader should determine how Pinker formalizes the semantic structures in chapter 5, which begins at file page 193 according to the table of contents at file page 9. The explicit representations of lexical rules and lexicosemantic structures are promised at file page 9, section 5.6. The learning mechanisms are summarized at file page 9, section 6.5. The developmental sequence and the unlearning problem are at file page 9, sections 7.1 and 7.2.

Three questions remain open for the thinking-machine design. First, how does the machine discover the narrow conflation classes from input, given that the boundaries are partly arbitrary and the search space may be large? Second, how does the machine represent and use temporal experience, which this section does not address? Third, how does the machine resolve perceptual ambiguity in the assignment of semantic elements, given that Pinker says language constrains the construal but does not describe the perceptual process that generates candidate construals? A fourth question, raised by the dialect differences at file page 138, is whether the machine should be designed to converge on one dialect or to represent variation. None of these is answered in the pages I have read.
